As part of the process of becoming an independent country, Botswana held its first election under universal suffrage in 1965. The Bechuanaland Democratic Party, led by Seretse Khama, won a gigantic landslide, with more than 80 percent of the vote. Khama later sat for an interview with the British press. When asked if he’d have preferred a smaller margin of victory, he agreed: “I think it’s healthy to have an opposition which is effective, because it keeps the government on its toes.”

Khama turned out to be an exceptionally gifted statesman, and today we see the wisdom of his statement in conservative states all across America. Trump touted big economic projects in two key Senate states this week. Both announcements soon crumbled | CNN Politics

President Donald Trump has made it abundantly clear that he’s happy to use official government resources in ethically dubious ways to try to win the 2026 midterm elections.

Actual Article Body:
President Donald Trump has made it abundantly clear that he’s happy to use official government resources in ethically dubious ways to try to win the 2026 midterm elections.

He promised to pay every adult US citizen $5,000 if Republicans win. He’s sending $500 to some Obamacare recipients with a very political letter enclosed. And now he’s running government-funded ads that promote himself and are obviously geared towards the election.

But wait. There’s more.

Twice this week, Trump has held White House events announcing a major economic project that happens to benefit a state holding a key, competitive Senate race — first in Iowa, then in Alaska.

And both times, his promises have proven to be overzealous, at best.

Trump announced the Iowa project on Monday at an Oval Office event featuring Senate candidate Rep. Ashley Hinson and many others
